title: A minimum age for social media

turns.speaker: Zoe
turns.text: So the under-sixteen ban is going ahead. Platforms have to verify age or they get fined.

turns.speaker: Stewart
turns.text: Verify age how, though? That's never the part anyone explains.

turns.speaker: Zoe
turns.text: Document upload, or face estimation from the camera.

turns.speaker: Priya
turns.text: So to protect children's privacy, everyone hands a photograph of their passport to a social media company.

turns.speaker: Stewart
turns.text: That did occur to me, yes.

turns.speaker: Zoe
turns.text: There are third-party checkers that don't pass the document on. It's not quite as bad as it sounds.

turns.speaker: Priya
turns.text: It's a database either way, and databases leak. But the bit I actually object to is that it treats sixteen like a switch. Nothing changes on that birthday.

turns.speaker: Stewart
turns.text: You could say that about drinking, driving, voting. We draw the line somewhere and it's always slightly arbitrary.

turns.speaker: Priya
turns.text: Although with driving there's a test. Here there's just a date.

turns.speaker: Zoe
turns.text: The strongest version of the case isn't really about harm to any one child. It's that as long as everyone's on it, no individual family can opt out. A ban makes the decision collectively.

turns.speaker: Stewart
turns.text: That's the only argument that's moved me at all, actually. It's a coordination problem, not a safety one.

turns.speaker: Priya
turns.text: I still think they'll all be on it within a month through somebody's older cousin.

points: A ban on social media for under-sixteens is proceeding, with fines for platforms that fail to verify age.
Verification means document upload or facial age estimation, which Priya argues undermines privacy for everyone.
Zoe notes third-party checkers exist that do not pass documents to the platform; Priya replies that any database can leak.
Priya's substantive objection is that sixteen is treated as a switch although nothing changes on that birthday.
Stewart compares it to drinking, driving and voting, where arbitrary lines are normal, though Priya notes driving at least requires a test.
Zoe gives the strongest case: while everyone is on the platform no single family can opt out, so a ban solves a coordination problem rather than a safety one.
